frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe seeks stable Algerian gas supplies while pressing for market access and political cooperation. Algiers is using long-term contracts and diversified partnerships to preserve control over its energy sector.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Libya, and Niger raises security costs and complicates Algeria's non-intervention posture. External military and intelligence activity near its borders remains a sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting strong US, EU, and Gulf interest because of its access to critical minerals. Luanda can gain leverage and investment, but must prevent corridor financing and logistics from eroding national control.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining production, foreign-operator dominance, and debt-linked obligations constrain Angola's policy autonomy. Diversification efforts are advancing but remain vulnerable to commodity-price and financing shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border and transit dispute
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger have disrupted cross-border trade and complicated use of Benin's port and pipeline infrastructure. The dispute exposes Benin to revenue losses and pressure from larger regional powers.

frictionVectors.title: Northern militant spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist activity spreading south from the Sahel is raising costs for roads, parks, and agricultural investment. Benin is expanding security partnerships while seeking to retain operational autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers partnership renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for a larger share of diamond value, marketing control, and domestic beneficiation. The negotiations test whether foreign capital remains compatible with stronger national resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Diversification financing gap
frictionVectors.details: Lithium, copper, and other mineral prospects are drawing external investors, but infrastructure and processing capacity remain limited. Botswana must avoid replacing diamond dependence with another externally controlled extractive model.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking greater state participation, local processing, and tighter oversight of gold exports. These measures may increase fiscal capture but risk deterring investment and encouraging informal or illicit production.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou's reliance on Russian-linked security support is reducing Western influence but creating a new external dependency. Persistent insurgency limits the state's ability to secure mines, transport corridors, and rural production zones.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state control over nickel, rare-earth and other mineral projects, but weak processing capacity and reliance on foreign capital limit value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Accusations involving armed groups and cross-border support keep relations with Rwanda tense, disrupting regional commerce and complicating sovereign control in the east.

frictionVectors.title: Port and connectivity dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde retains strong institutional control over its infrastructure, but ports, telecommunications and energy systems remain dependent on European, Chinese and multilateral financing.

frictionVectors.title: Blue-economy security gap
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and transnational trafficking challenge control of the country's extensive maritime zone, where enforcement capacity remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and mining value leakage
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbons, timber and emerging mining projects generate state revenue but remain exposed to foreign operators, opaque contracting and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and northern insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside Boko Haram-linked threats in the Far North, weakens infrastructure security and state access to affected areas.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-resource nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel remain central to regime protection, while allegations persist that access to mining and commercial concessions influences the relationship.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-group territorial control
frictionVectors.details: Rebel and criminal networks continue to contest roads, borderlands and mining zones, limiting Bangui's ability to regulate resources or guarantee infrastructure corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal autonomy remains highly exposed to oil production, foreign technical operators and export infrastructure beyond its borders, especially the pipeline corridor to Cameroon.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Sudan border pressure
frictionVectors.details: Instability spilling from Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic diverts state capacity toward security and threatens transport, trade and resource infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: France–Comoros territorial friction
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved status of Mayotte continues to constrain relations with France and complicate maritime sovereignty, migration management, and access to surrounding resources.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure dependency
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic capital leaves ports, energy, and connectivity projects dependent on foreign donors and investors, reducing national leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral supply-chain competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt assets attract intense competition among Chinese, Western, and regional actors, while weak oversight limits the state’s ability to capture full value from extraction.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and regional security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to erode Kinshasa’s territorial authority and exposes mineral corridors to armed groups, neighboring-state interests, and competing external security initiatives.

highlights: Oil anchors a narrow sovereignty base

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: State revenues and foreign-exchange capacity remain heavily tied to oil, leaving Brazzaville vulnerable to price cycles and the bargaining power of international energy firms.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Major roads, rail, and port projects involving Chinese finance and contractors improve connectivity but can narrow fiscal and policy autonomy when debt service pressures rise.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Côte d’Ivoire remains a major cocoa producer but captures less value than downstream foreign processors and brands, sustaining pressure for greater domestic processing and pricing power.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign investment leverage
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and offshore energy investment strengthen growth, yet reliance on multinational capital creates continuing exposure to external commercial and regulatory influence.

highlights: Port geography remains a strategic asset

frictionVectors.title: Military-base competition
frictionVectors.details: The concentration of foreign military facilities gives Djibouti revenue and diplomatic leverage, but also makes its security environment dependent on rival external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Port infrastructure and trade corridors tied to external financing provide essential income while increasing vulnerability to creditor pressure and competition from neighboring regional hubs.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt remains locked in a strategic dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and downstream water guarantees. Cairo is pursuing diplomatic and regional pressure while avoiding an open military confrontation.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF support and substantial Gulf investment strengthen short-term stability but give external partners greater influence over state assets, privatization, and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Revenue Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil and gas output is narrowing fiscal space while foreign operators and offshore infrastructure remain central to production. The state retains formal control but has limited capacity to replace external capital and technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: China-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction have expanded ports, roads, and urban infrastructure, increasing Malabo's dependence on external contractors and commodity-linked repayment arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide hard currency but rely heavily on foreign firms, imported expertise, and opaque production agreements. This strengthens state revenue while limiting broad-based domestic control of the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline remains strategically valuable amid competition involving Gulf states, Türkiye, Egypt, and Ethiopia. External security partnerships can enhance regime leverage but also expose Asmara to regional bargaining pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on South African Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies on South Africa for major transport routes, electricity linkages, trade access, and financial connectivity. Disruptions or policy shifts in Pretoria can quickly constrain Mbabane's economic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Preferential Trade Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Sugar and textile exports remain vulnerable to changes in regional and international trade preferences. External market access supports employment but limits sovereign control over industrial strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD has strengthened Ethiopia's control over its electricity and water infrastructure while intensifying tensions with Egypt and Sudan. Addis Ababa continues to frame the project as a sovereign development asset, complicating regional compromise.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Internal Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, IMF-linked reforms, and dependence on foreign investment constrain policy autonomy. Persistent insecurity in Amhara, Oromia, and other areas also threatens transport corridors, power projects, and resource development.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and local processing in manganese, iron ore, and oil. This may improve sovereign control but risks tensions with established foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon remains dependent on foreign capital and expertise for the Owendo and mineral-export logistics chain. Disruptions or concession disputes could quickly affect state revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Cross-Border Trade Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for overland trade, food flows, and access to regional markets. Border frictions or transport restrictions could expose the country's limited strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Resource Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fishing and weak monitoring continue to constrain national control over fisheries. Limited enforcement capacity also increases the risk of revenue loss and coastal insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Foreign Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining is degrading water systems and undermining state control over mineral revenues. Foreign-linked trading networks and smuggling complicate efforts to formalize the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking more domestic value addition in gold, lithium, and other minerals while balancing investor demands and fiscal constraints. Debt restructuring and IMF-backed reforms narrow the government's room to impose tougher terms.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Infrastructure Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project is drawing major foreign capital and promises transformative rail and port construction. Guinea's leverage is substantial, but financing, timelines, and revenue-sharing remain dependent on external consortia.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Enclave Economics
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite exports remain dominated by foreign operators with limited domestic processing. The authorities are pressing for infrastructure and local-content gains, but state capacity and political uncertainty constrain enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Cashew Trade
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains highly dependent on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and the state exposed to foreign buyers, price volatility, and limited processing capacity. This weakens domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Influence
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's port and coastal waters are vulnerable to foreign commercial influence, illicit trafficking, and unregulated fishing. Weak institutions limit the government's ability to secure maritime resources or negotiate balanced infrastructure agreements.

highlights: Ports and energy remain strategic battlegrounds

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL DEBT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and major bilateral creditors constrain Nairobi's room to direct infrastructure and social spending. Debt-service pressure keeps Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing strategically influential.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND POWER COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and regional transport corridors attract competing Gulf, Chinese, and Western interests. Energy import dependence and grid-financing needs add further external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: HIGHLANDS WATER CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project provides vital revenue and leverage, but its infrastructure and market are overwhelmingly tied to South Africa. Construction delays, security concerns, and unequal bargaining power limit Maseru's autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: TEXTILE AND CUSTOMS EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's garment sector depends heavily on external buyers and preferential trade access, particularly through the United States. Any changes to trade preferences or regional customs rules can rapidly affect employment and fiscal stability.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign mining concessions dominate export earnings and infrastructure decisions, leaving Liberia exposed to commodity cycles and bargaining asymmetries. The government is seeking stronger local content and revenue collection without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and mining corridors rely on foreign operators, contractors, and financing. Concession terms and control of transport infrastructure remain recurring sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: OIL GOVERNANCE FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Rival political authorities and armed networks continue to contest control over oil revenues, appointments, and export infrastructure. The National Oil Corporation remains a key national institution but operates under intense political pressure.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN MILITARY FOOTPRINTS
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked forces, and regional actors retain influence through security partnerships, bases, arms, and political relationships. Their presence limits unified Libyan control over strategic territory and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and technical operators. Revenue disputes, environmental impacts, and limited domestic processing constrain Madagascar's control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND INFRASTRUCTURE GAP
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and weak transport links make the state dependent on external lenders and concessionaires. Infrastructure financing can improve capacity but often comes with limited local control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: IMF CONDITIONALITY
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-backed reforms are stabilizing external accounts but constrain fiscal autonomy and public investment. Malawi remains highly exposed to imported fuel, fertilizer, and food costs.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND POWER BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in uranium, rare-earth, and other mineral projects is rising faster than regulatory capacity. Chronic electricity shortages and weak transmission infrastructure limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: The transition government relies heavily on Russian security assistance while seeking greater control over gold and other strategic resources. This reduces Western influence but creates dependence on an alternative external power.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACT CONFRONTATIONS
frictionVectors.details: Disputes with international mining firms over taxation, ownership, and operating conditions threaten production and investor confidence. Insecurity around mining zones further raises logistics and sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN-CONTROLLED GAS INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and foreign operators offers major revenue potential but leaves Mauritania dependent on external capital, technology, and export infrastructure. Revenue-sharing and local-content arrangements will shape perceived sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND CORRIDOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: SNIM remains central to the economy, while Chinese and other foreign partners influence iron-ore logistics and processing. Weak inland transport and Sahel insecurity constrain diversification into higher-value minerals and green hydrogen.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS AND DIEGO GARCIA
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius has strengthened its sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago while managing the strategic reality of the Diego Garcia base. The issue remains sensitive because it involves British and US security interests.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN INFRASTRUCTURE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Port, digital, and maritime investments attract competing Indian, Chinese, Gulf, and Western interests. Mauritius must preserve its role as a financial and logistics hub without becoming overdependent on any one external partner.

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Control and development of Western Sahara underpin Morocco's territorial strategy and attract investment, but generate persistent legal and diplomatic friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front, and some European actors.

frictionVectors.title: GREEN HYDROGEN AND WATER PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed renewable and green-hydrogen projects could expand Morocco's strategic autonomy while creating dependence on external technology, export markets, and financing. Severe water stress remains a constraint on industrial and agricultural sovereignty.

highlights: LNG revival tied to foreign protection

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to constrain state authority around gas projects and transport corridors. Mozambican forces remain dependent on regional and external security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms retain substantial influence over project timelines, financing, and security conditions. Gas revenues could strengthen sovereignty, but only if fiscal terms and local participation improve.

highlights: Green hydrogen seeks national value capture

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms dominate the capital and technical capacity needed to develop offshore oil finds. Namibia is pressing for stronger state participation and domestic processing to avoid a narrow enclave economy.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, lithium, and rare-earth projects attract competing Chinese, European, and Gulf interests. Infrastructure and export agreements will determine whether Namibia captures broader strategic value.

highlights: Uranium and oil face security pressure

frictionVectors.title: Russian and Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The junta has reduced French influence but remains reliant on external military partnerships and vulnerable regional borders. This shifts leverage rather than fully resolving Niger's security dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Export Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency, sanctions legacies, and transport constraints threaten uranium and oil operations. The state has greater political control over concessions but weaker capacity to secure and monetize them consistently.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Vandalism, theft, and militant activity continue to reduce production and public revenue. Foreign operators retain major technical and financial influence while communities contest local environmental and fiscal outcomes.

frictionVectors.title: Refinery and Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Domestic refining expansion could improve energy sovereignty, but fuel markets remain exposed to imported products, foreign exchange shortages, and opaque trading networks. Infrastructure bottlenecks continue to dilute the benefits of crude ownership.

highlights: Eastern Congo ties raise external pressure

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Mineral Allegations
frictionVectors.details: Accusations that Rwanda benefits from mineral flows linked to eastern Congo create diplomatic and sanctions exposure. Kigali seeks to preserve its role as a regional logistics and processing hub while denying facilitation of armed groups.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Security Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong state control but remains sensitive to Western aid conditions and shifting regional security partnerships. External scrutiny can affect infrastructure finance, mineral access, and military diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Resource Competition
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe is balancing offshore oil hopes with limited negotiating capacity and uncertainty over commercially viable reserves. External energy firms and neighboring states retain substantial influence over maritime resource development.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country depends heavily on external partners for port modernization, maritime surveillance, and infrastructure finance. This creates exposure to strategic competition in the Gulf of Guinea.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas revenues are strengthening Dakar's bargaining position, but contract reviews and local-content demands risk friction with international operators and lenders. Managing expectations over public benefits remains politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure commitments and fiscal constraints limit Senegal's room to direct resource revenues toward sovereign priorities. Chinese, Gulf, European, and multilateral financing all remain influential.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on foreign partners, particularly India and other maritime-security providers, for surveillance, coast-guard support, and infrastructure. The government must preserve strategic autonomy while protecting its exclusive economic zone.

frictionVectors.title: Tuna Value-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Fishing and transshipment revenues remain vulnerable to foreign fleet access, changing quotas, and climate pressures. Limited domestic processing capacity reduces the share of maritime value retained locally.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Rutile Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Sierra Leone's fiscal and export position remains highly exposed to foreign mining operators and volatile commodity prices. Local-content and revenue-sharing efforts have improved bargaining leverage but have not displaced the extractive structure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Influence
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors, port logistics, and power infrastructure attract competing foreign investors and lenders. Concession terms and environmental impacts remain potential sources of domestic political friction.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil and License Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Somalia is seeking to develop offshore hydrocarbons, but weak institutions, disputed licensing authority, and unresolved federal-regional tensions complicate effective sovereign control. Foreign operators and neighboring states remain important to exploration and maritime enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Port Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Gulf states, and other partners are shaping port, logistics, and security infrastructure. These arrangements provide essential capacity but can deepen political fragmentation and limit unified national control.

highlights: Power and rail constraints limit leverage

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic mining
frictionVectors.details: International firms and investors remain central to platinum, manganese, chromium and battery-mineral development. Efforts to expand local beneficiation face regulatory uncertainty, infrastructure bottlenecks and capital shortages.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics and electricity degradation
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable rail, ports and electricity reduce South Africa's ability to capture value from its mineral base. State recovery efforts are increasingly dependent on private capital and external technology.

highlights: Peace remains vulnerable to armed fragmentation

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence and oil disruption
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on Sudanese export infrastructure, leaving its principal revenue stream exposed to conflict, transit disputes and external operators. Production and fiscal stability remain highly vulnerable to pipeline insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: Regional and elite competition over resources
frictionVectors.details: Political factions, neighboring states and commercial networks compete for control of oil revenues, gold and transport corridors. Weak institutions limit the state's ability to convert resource wealth into sovereign development.

highlights: War fragments control of gold and ports

frictionVectors.title: Gold networks and wartime extraction
frictionVectors.details: Competing military and commercial networks control major gold flows, with foreign buyers and intermediaries helping sustain armed actors. This diverts revenue from national institutions and deepens external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access, maritime facilities and logistics corridors are strategic targets for regional and international powers. Control of these assets is increasingly tied to military bargaining rather than coherent national development.

highlights: Ports and gas corridors attract rival partners

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking stronger fiscal, domestic-supply and local-content terms in developing its offshore gas resources. Negotiations with international energy companies remain sensitive to project delays and financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam and proposed regional transport links draw investment from China, Gulf actors and Western partners. The government must balance infrastructure access with concerns over debt, concessions and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a Gulf of Guinea transshipment and regional trade hub depends on foreign shipping, finance and infrastructure expertise. This generates revenue but leaves strategic logistics assets exposed to external commercial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover and corridor security
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and political instability across the northern frontier threaten transport routes and state presence. Togo is expanding security cooperation while trying to avoid excessive dependence on any single outside partner.

frictionVectors.title: EU MIGRATION AND FINANCE BARGAIN
frictionVectors.details: European financial and migration cooperation gives Brussels significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Delays in external financing increase pressure on the government to secure alternatives without deepening dependency.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND PHOSPHATE CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: High energy-import costs weaken fiscal sovereignty, while phosphate-sector disruptions limit export earnings. Domestic production and infrastructure bottlenecks remain more important than direct foreign control.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP AND TRANSNATIONAL OIL CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Uganda retains ownership stakes and expects major revenues, but TotalEnergies, CNOOC, and export infrastructure partners shape project financing, technology, and timelines. Environmental, land-rights, and sanctions-related pressure continues to constrain national policy space.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT-FUNDED INFRASTRUCTURE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Large transport and energy projects deepen reliance on foreign lenders and contractors. Kampala is seeking to balance Chinese infrastructure ties with Gulf, Western, and regional partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL-MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using copper and cobalt importance to attract competing US, European, Chinese, and Gulf investment while pursuing more local processing. Ownership structures, tax terms, and supply-chain access remain vulnerable to external bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: ELECTRICITY AND GRID FRAGILITY
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortfalls and drought-related generation losses constrain mining and manufacturing. Emergency imports and new generation projects create additional exposure to regional power markets and foreign financiers.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CAPITAL AND RESOURCE ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors remain central to lithium, platinum, gold, and coal development, giving external firms substantial influence over capital, technology, and export channels. Harare's beneficiation rules improve formal control but have not eliminated opaque ownership and revenue risks.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT, SANCTIONS, AND CURRENCY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Arrears, limited access to conventional finance, and currency instability reduce Zimbabwe's ability to negotiate from strength. The government increasingly relies on resource-backed investment and non-Western partners, which can narrow transparency and fiscal-policy options.
